questions.title: What is the exact definition of a 'law‑enforcement purpose' under FOIA Exemption 7(A), and how does that apply to an FBI file that includes both investigative notes and immigration‑related documents?
questions.question_body: The opinion states that the FBI ‘carried its burden to show that Farahi’s file was compiled for law‑enforcement purposes.’  However, the file contains not only investigation notes but also immigration‑related documents and commentary from an immigration hearing.  How do courts discriminate between records that are truly ‘compiled for law‑enforcement purposes’ and those that are merely administrative or immigration‑related?  Does the presence of any law‑enforcement–related content automatically render the entire file subject to Exemption 7(A)?

questions.title: How do courts determine whether an investigation is still 'pending or reasonably anticipated,' especially when time has elapsed since the original FOIA request?
questions.question_body: In this case, the Bender declaration was brief and essentially reiterated that the investigation remains ongoing.  Yet Farahi argues that the time lapse casts doubt on the continuation of enforcement proceedings.  What factual evidence must the government provide to satisfy the standard that proceedings are still pending or reasonably anticipated?  Are ongoing investigations automatically considered pending, or is a more detailed, time‑specific analysis required?

questions.title: When does the FOIA ‘reasonable segregability’ standard allow for partial release of an otherwise exempt record?
questions.question_body: The court concluded that no portion of the 10,750 pages and 80 CDs was reasonably segregable because the exempt material was “inextricably intertwined.”  What specific factors does a court look for to assess segregability?  Must the exempt content completely dominate each page, or can a single paragraph or line within a document be isolated?  How does the court balance the need to preserve law‑enforcement evidence against the public’s right to access non‑exempt information?

questions.title: What is the scope of deference given to agencies when invoking FOIA Exemption 7(A), especially in national‑security contexts?
questions.question_body: The opinion repeatedly cites deference to the FBI’s determination that a record is compiled for law‑enforcement purposes.  How far does that deference extend to the agency’s assertion that information could ‘reasonably be expected to interfere with enforcement proceedings’?  Are agencies allowed to rely on broad, high‑level statements (e.g., ‘investigations remain ongoing’) without more granular evidence, or must they provide detailed factual corroboration?

questions.title: What are the requirements for category‑by‑category withholding under FOIA, and why did the court find Farahi’s challenge to the categories ‘unavailing’?
questions.question_body: Farahi objected that the FBI used overbroad categories without explanation.  The court said he forfeited that argument because he offered no specific reasoning for overbreadth.  What standard does a plaintiff need to meet to succeed in a category‑by‑category withholding challenge?  Must the agency justify each category?  How does the court determine whether a category is wide enough to conceal exempt material?

questions.title: What is the procedural value of ex‑parte affidavits in FOIA cases, and can they be challenged on the public record?
questions.question_body: The FBI’s update was an ex‑parte affidavit, and the court relied on it heavily, yet Farahi could not contest it on the public record.  Under what circumstances is it permissible for a court to accept an ex‑parte declaration without a hearing?  When can a plaintiff raise objections to the adequacy or sufficiency of an ex‑parte declaration?  How does this balance the need to protect sensitive information with the FOIA’s transparency purpose?

questions.title: How does the FOIA exemption framework handle the interplay between Exemption 7(A) and the requirement to release ‘reasonably segregable’ portions?
questions.question_body: The opinion notes that the government must disclose any reasonably segregable portion of a record.  But if Exemption 7(A) applies to the entire record, does that automatically preclude the release of non‑exempt material even if it is interleaved?  What are the precedents for partial disclosure when part of a record is exempt but part is not?

questions.title: What is the impact of the passage of time on the plain‑text “likely interference” analysis under Exemption 7(A)?
questions.question_body: The court cited CREW that a vague assertion of ongoing investigations might not suffice, yet ended up accepting a brief declaration.  How does the passage of time influence the factual assessment of whether disclosure could interfere with future enforcement?  Are there specific statutory or case‑law thresholds for determining when an investigation is considered ‘overdue’ or ‘to be concluded’?

questions.title: How do FOIA courts distinguish between ‘law‑enforcement duties’ and ‘security‑related duties’ when applying Exemption 7(A)?
questions.question_body: The opinion references that the FBI’s determination was entitled to deference, especially for national‑security concerns.  Does a security‑related investigation automatically confer deference, or must the agency still demonstrate a clear nexus to a traditional law‑enforcement duty?  How do courts reconcile a broader privacy or national‑security interest with the statutory requirement of a ‘law‑enforcement purpose’?
